title: Cardiac Syncope with Anoxic Seizure Activity
case_prompt:
A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope on standing from a crouched position. She reported dizziness and lightheadedness before loss of consciousness; witnesses described 3–5 minutes of limb jerking, eye rolling, and urinary incontinence. On recovery she complained of a bifrontal headache. Her history included asthma, psoriasis, and recent initiation of citalopram for possible depression. She had previously been evaluated for ventricular bigeminy. She was a nonsmoker and drank minimally.

On examination, blood pressure was 95/61 mmHg and heart rate was 50 bpm; the remainder of her cardiac and neurologic examinations was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG on admission showed sinus rhythm with monomorphic premature ventricular complexes. Shortly after arrival, she had a second collapse characterized by stertorous breathing, hypertonia of the upper limbs, bradycardia, and transient postictal hypertension; she denied chest pain or palpitations prior to this event.

Noncontrast head CT and CT venogram revealed no acute hemorrhage or venous thrombosis but identified a small developmental venous anomaly. During CT imaging she developed a cardiac arrest but regained spontaneous circulation after chest compressions. Subsequent ECG monitoring revealed runs of nonsustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Laboratory studies, including serum electrolytes, were within normal limits. She was treated with intravenous magnesium sulfate, temporary pacing to suppress ventricular ectopy, and citalopram was discontinued. Review of serial ECGs showed a corrected QT interval at the upper limit of normal or mildly prolonged (470–504 ms), although precise measurement was hampered by frequent ectopic beats.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurogenic syncope secondary to subarachnoid hemorrhage was considered but excluded by imaging showing no hemorrhage — “Her CT head and subsequent CT venogram did not show an acute bleed or venous sinus thrombosis.”  
2. Torsades de pointes from citalopram-induced QT prolongation was considered, but the evidence for significant QTc prolongation was weak — “the working diagnosis until that time from the emergency clinicians was of PMVT secondary to prolonged QTc induced by citalopram even though our evidence of a prolonged QTc was fairly weak.”  
3. Structural heart disease was excluded after imaging demonstrated normal coronary arteries and cardiac anatomy — “coronary angiography and cardiac MRI which were both normal.”  
4. Accessory pathway–mediated tachycardia was ruled out by electrophysiological testing — “electrophysiology studies that ruled out the presence of an accessory pathway.”  
5. Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia was suspected based on the emergence of bidirectional PVCs — “PVCs of multiple morphologies that at one point looked bidirectional, raising the possibility of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.”
